newsitem.title: INDIA: India sugar de-control to boost long-term exports.
newsitem.headline: India sugar de-control to boost long-term exports.

text.p: India's decision to end a trading agency's monopoly of sugar exports could push up overseas sales in the long term but was unlikely to generate immediate gains, analysts said on Wednesday.
"In the long run it will have an impact as market forces will operate...As of now it is only a psychological satisfaction," said Charan Wadhwa, economist at the Centre for Policy Research.
Indian President Shankar Dayal Sharma on Monday approved an ordinance to end the export monopoly of the Indian Sugar and General Industries Import-Export Corp (ISGIEC).
The ordinance was issued after a government-backed bill to end the monopoly failed to clear parliament before it adjourned in late December.
Wadhwa told Reuters the government measure was unlikely to generate immediate gains, and perhaps not for as long as five years.
He said sugar was a highly politicised commodity in India and a package of measures was needed to get the best from the industry. Sugar supplies and pricing in India are controlled by the government.
The mills supply 40 percent of their output as levy at a subsidised rate for distribution among the poor and sell the rest in the open market.

India began abolishing licences for many industries under a reform programme that began in 1991, but it kept sugar under the old regime, which has subsidised prices for consumers and protected producers.
Sugar industry officials said the government's decision might backfire on an industry whose costs are higher than international prices.
They said the move could lead to competing mills undercutting on export prices, and export sales drying up as traders were exposed to mounting losses.
Under the current system, losses incurred by ISGIEC on exports were borne by sugar factories on the basis of allotments made to them for exports, they said.
They said the cost of producing sugar in India was higher than the export prices because of government controls.

"In the short-term scenario it is good to have one agency to avoid undercutting but as a policy it is better to have a free regime for trade," said Shashank Bhide of the National Council of Applied Economic Research.
Bhide said making small changes might not help and what was required was a policy for the entire sugar sector.
Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told parliament in December that the new measure would ensure production of good quality sugar and allow mills to export directly.
India produced an all-time high of 16.4 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96 (October-September) and the new season started with stocks as high as 8.1 million tonnes, government officials said.
India exported a little more than one million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96.
Deve Gowda said last month some 3.5 million tonnes of sugar were stored that India wanted to sell.
